original_question: (Well-known problem). A finite group G is called an IYB-group if it is isomorphic to the permutation group of a finite involutive non-degenerate set-theoretic solution of the Yang–Baxter equation, or equivalently, G is isomorphic to the multiplicative group of a finite left brace. Assume that the Sylow subgroups of a finite soluble group G are IYB-groups. Is G an IYB-group?
target_in_paper: Problem 21.7 ("Well-known problem") in the 21st-issue update of arXiv:1401.0300, The Kourovka Notebook.
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's official problem statement almost verbatim. It correctly includes the paper's definition of an IYB-group, the finite soluble hypothesis on G, the assumption on Sylow subgroups, and the precise yes/no question being asked.
missing_details: For full stand-alone clarity, make the standard group-theoretic quantifier explicit: for every prime p dividing |G|, a Sylow p-subgroup of G is assumed to be an IYB-group.
refined_question: Let G be a finite soluble group. Suppose that for every prime p dividing |G|, a Sylow p-subgroup of G is an involutive Yang-Baxter group; that is, each such Sylow subgroup is isomorphic to the permutation group of a finite involutive non-degenerate set-theoretic solution of the Yang-Baxter equation, equivalently, to the multiplicative group of a finite left brace. Must G itself be an involutive Yang-Baxter group?
justification: In arXiv:1401.0300, the draft is not merely close to the intended target: it is essentially the official wording of Problem 21.7. The paper does not frame this as a broader conjecture in a nearby theorem/proposition chain; rather, it records exactly this narrow open problem. Therefore the sharpest paper-faithful refinement is to preserve the statement and only make the Sylow-subgroup quantifier explicit, without broadening it to the neighboring but stronger question of whether all finite soluble groups are IYB-groups.
